An introduction

I collect light the way some people collect places — before the hills have finished waking, and after the city has switched itself on. Everything here happened in those hours, when the world lowers its voice.

Twenty-one years old. Raised in Khammam, drawn to hill roads, early fog, old fabric, and engines that idle like a heartbeat. None of these frames were staged for anyone else — they are simply the record of paying attention.

Read this page the way you would walk through a small exhibition: slowly, out of order if you like, and without asking the photographs to explain themselves.

Chapter I

Mistwhere the hills exhale

Cold mornings above the tree line. The fog arrives before you do and leaves after — you learn to stand still inside it.

Two horses, one field, and a sun that took its time. Nobody spoke. Nobody needed to.

The hills don't perform. That's the whole appeal. You climb, you wait, you let the temperature write on your skin — and if the fog decides to open, you get thirty seconds of a view no photograph fully keeps.

“The quietest hours built the loudest parts of me — discipline is just patience, repeated until it looks like luck.”
Syed Abraar Mohiuddin — margin note, age twenty-one

Two hundred kilograms off the floor — proof that patience, eventually, gets heavy.Deadlift · 200 kg · lockout

Chapter III

Threadwhat heritage feels like

Kurta cotton, a borrowed shawl, festival evenings. Some clothes are worn; these are inherited — even when they're new.

There is a version of me that only exists in these clothes. Straighter spine, slower walk, the sense of standing inside a long line of men who dressed like this for mornings that mattered.

Eid at home. A paddy field the colour of a green nobody has bottled yet. A shawl thrown on for one photograph and kept on for the rest of the day. Heritage isn't a costume — it's a temperature.

Asphaltbetween departures
